"""layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1408 -- a "therefore / confident deduction" direction.

What the component does: when it is strongly positive it sits on words that
introduce a conclusion ("Therefore", "Thus", "Hence", sentence-initial "So"),
and it is mildly positive on plain modal and copula words ("is", "will", "should",
"need", "because"). It is negative on hesitation and contrast words ("however",
"but", "or", "perhaps", "might", "if"). Its output direction, read through the
unembedding, promotes "must / need / legitimately" and suppresses "perhaps /
maybe / might / seems", so the sign tracks confident deduction versus hedging.

What this program predicts: a value per token from those word groups, using only
the current token and the one before it. It has no memory across tokens. The
group values are the mean activations measured on training text.

It explains only a small part of the activation. Most of its variance is a
diffuse, token-local spread (about +/-0.6) that these word lists do not capture.
"""
READS = ()

# Words that introduce a conclusion: strongly positive.
CONCLUDE = {"therefore", "thus", "hence", "consequently", "accordingly",
            "因此", "所以", "だから", "donc", "поэтому", "从而", "故"}
# Copulas and modals: mildly positive.
AUX = {"is", "are", "was", "were", "will", "should", "must", "have", "has", "can", "be", "need"}
# Reason words and contractions: mildly positive.
REASON = {"because", "then", "'s", "’s", "'m", "’m", "'re", "’re", "'ll", "’ll"}
# Hedges and contrast words: slightly negative.
HEDGE = {"perhaps", "maybe", "might", "possibly", "seems", "seem", "seemed", "may", "could",
         "likely", "probably"}
CONTRAST = {"however", "but", "although", "though", "while", "or", "if", "alternatively", "yet",
            "whereas"}
# Tokens after which a "so" starts a clause (a conclusion), not "so that" / "is so".
CLAUSE_START = {",", ".", "and", "(", ")", "?", "!", ";", ":", ""}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if prefix.position > 0 else ""
    if word in CONCLUDE:
        value = 3.6
    elif word == "so":
        value = 3.2 if before in CLAUSE_START else 1.0
    elif word in AUX:
        value = 0.3
    elif word in REASON:
        value = 0.6
    elif word in HEDGE or word in CONTRAST:
        value = -0.1
    else:
        value = 0.08
    return carry, value

"""Activation of one MLP down-projection component in layer 15 of Qwen3-1.7B.

What it does, in plain terms
- Mostly it is a dense, diffuse feature: on ordinary text it wobbles around 0 (std ~0.35),
  and no token or context rule explains that wobble. The program leaves it at 0 there.
- Its readable behaviour is at the chat template's markup tokens, the tags that open and
  close turns, thinking and tool calls. Each has a typical value:
  * `<|im_start|>` (start of a turn) about -1.6;
  * `<tool_response>` about -2.1, `</tool_response>` about -0.5;
  * `<tool_call>` about -0.5, `</tool_call>` about -0.9;
  * `<think>` about -0.5, `</think>` about +0.6;
  * `<|im_end|>` (end of a turn) about +0.5.
- A document's first token is ~0. The token right after a document-initial `<|im_start|>`
  is about -1.7, and exactly -2.87 when it is `user`: with only two tokens of context,
  the value is fixed.

Documents are tracked by their labels: the position within a document resets at each
boundary, as the model's attention does.
"""

READS = ()

# typical activation of each markup token, averaged over training text
VALUES = {
    "<|im_start|>": -1.6,
    "<|im_end|>": 0.5,
    "<tool_response>": -2.1,
    "</tool_response>": -0.5,
    "<tool_call>": -0.5,
    "</tool_call>": -0.9,
    "<think>": -0.5,
    "</think>": 0.6,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document label, position of the previous token within its document)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or doc != carry[0]:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if pos == 0:
        value = 0.0
    elif pos == 1 and prefix.token_strings[-2] == "<|im_start|>":
        value = -2.87 if tok == "user" else -1.7
    else:
        value = VALUES.get(tok, 0.0)
    return (doc, pos), float(value)

"""Chat-structure delimiter detector with a small negative case for numbers
after an opening bracket: layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1410.

The component writes strongly positive values on the tokens that mark the
boundaries of chat turns, tool calls, tool results and reasoning blocks:
<|im_start|>, <|im_end|>, <tool_call>, </tool_call>, <tool_response>,
</tool_response>, <think>, </think>. Each gets its typical size (closing
tags and <|im_end|> after a tool result are largest).

It is negative on a lone space that sits right after an opening bracket or
a colon-newline, where the text is about to show a number ("PASSED [ 35%]",
"Statements   : 75% (", "# array([[ 0, 1 ...").
Every other token is predicted as 0, and the first token of each document is 0 too.
"""

READS = ()

# typical activation on each delimiter (means measured on training text)
DELIMITER_VALUE = {
    "<|im_start|>": 15.0,
    "<|im_end|>": 11.0,
    "<tool_call>": 13.7,
    "</tool_call>": 15.9,
    "<tool_response>": 11.5,
    "</tool_response>": 19.0,
    "<think>": 11.5,
    "</think>": 19.5,
}
# a space right after one of these is about to introduce a number
OPENERS = {" [", " (", ":\n"}
OPENER_SPACE_VALUE = -8.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # the first token of a document (or of the row) reads as 0
    new_doc = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if new_doc:
        return carry, 0.0
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token in DELIMITER_VALUE:
        return carry, DELIMITER_VALUE[token]
    if token == " " and prefix.token_strings[-2] in OPENERS:
        return carry, OPENER_SPACE_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 1411: a near-inert, noise-like readout.

What it does, in plain terms:
- At the first token of every document (and the first token of a row) it is exactly 0.
- Everywhere else it sits at its typical small negative level, about -0.047.

What it does NOT do: its activation is not explained by the current token, the
previous token, the position in the document, whether the token repeats earlier text,
or the character category of the token. Those features together explain essentially
none of its variance (held-out R^2 about 0.0003 for the category table). Its
causal importance is ~0 everywhere, so switching it off barely changes the model.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL = -0.047  # the component's average activation away from document starts


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    starts_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or (
        prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_doc else TYPICAL

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1412: a near-constant, context-driven readout.

What it is: the component's activation is almost entirely one MLP hidden unit of layer 15
(unit 1412, about half of its variance). That hidden unit is barely predictable from the
prefix: the current token, the previous token, word class, position in the document,
repetition and slowly-decaying counts of token types each explain at most about 1% of its
variance, and its direct effect on the output logits is diffuse, with no clear set of
promoted or suppressed tokens. Its activation has mean about -0.05 and std 0.42 and is
(essentially) exactly zero at the first token of each document, which has no earlier context.

What this program does: it predicts the average level (-0.05) at every token of a document,
and zero at the document's first token. It captures only that level and the document-start
zero; the per-token variation is not explained by anything in the prefix that is simple
enough to write down. A program with a real per-token rule would need the layer's
attention and MLP state, which a readable program cannot reproduce.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.05
"""The component's average activation over ordinary positions."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # The first token of a document has no earlier context: the component is silent there.
    first = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    return None, 0.0 if first else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Predicts component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1413 (layer 15 MLP down_proj).

This component is essentially unexplained by anything a short program can see.
Its activation is dense noise-like text-dependent signal (std ~0.32) with a small
negative mean, and no token identity, token class, previous token, repetition or
position feature explains more than ~0.3% of its variance.

The one clean fact: at the first token of each document (or row start) the component
is silent (activation ~0). Everywhere else we predict its typical small negative mean.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL_ACTIVATION = -0.04  # the component's mean over ordinary tokens


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    starts_document = prefix.position == 0 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_document else TYPICAL_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1414, as read by its down_proj component, as a few text rules.

The component is almost exactly one MLP hidden unit of layer 15 (its input direction is that
unit alone), so its activation is that unit's value times the size of its output direction.
The unit is large and positive at line breaks: most of all the line break that ends a chat
turn ("<|im_end|>" or "assistant" then "\\n"), and then line breaks in running prose, more so
after a long line. Line breaks inside code are slightly negative. The end of a document
(<|endoftext|>) is negative, more so deep into a document. Every other token sits near zero,
slightly negative. The rules below predict those values; they explain only a few percent of
the variance, because most of the activation's size is not visible in the text.
"""

READS = ()

ROLE_TOKENS = ("<|im_end|>", "<|im_start|>", "assistant")
CODE_CHARS = set(";{}()[]<>=")
WINDOW = 32  # tokens of the same document looked at for the line length and code test
CODE_SHARE = 0.2  # share of code-like tokens in the window that makes it code


def _is_code(recent):
    hits = sum(1 for s in recent if any(c in CODE_CHARS for c in s))
    return bool(recent) and hits / len(recent) >= CODE_SHARE


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = prefix.position
    cur = tokens[-1]
    # this document's tokens before the current one, up to WINDOW of them
    start = len(docs) - 1
    while start > 0 and docs[start - 1] == docs[-1] and len(docs) - start < WINDOW:
        start -= 1
    recent = tokens[start:-1]
    if cur == "<|endoftext|>":
        return carry, -0.6 - 0.5 * min(t, 300) / 100
    if "\n" in cur:
        if len(tokens) > 1 and tokens[-2] in ROLE_TOKENS:
            return carry, 3.0  # the line break that ends a chat turn
        if _is_code(recent):
            return carry, -0.2  # a line break in code
        line = 0  # tokens since the last line break, up to WINDOW
        for s in reversed(recent):
            if "\n" in s:
                break
            line += 1
        return carry, 0.2 + min(line, 60) / 60  # a line break in prose
    return carry, -0.05

"""Activity verbs of everyday personal life (read, eat, drink, buy, wear, live, play, learn,
write, own, sell, run, ...) and "of" after owner or transfer nouns ("owner of", "author of",
"sale of").

What the component does: it reads the MLP hidden state of layer 15, and about half of its
input weight sits on one hidden unit. Its largest values fall on a verb for something a
person does with concrete things, when a person or a modal/"to" comes just before it: "you
can also [read]", "I [drink]", "who [live]", "to [learn]". The same word after a determiner
or possessive ("his reading", "the play") is near zero. Most other words, including the
program's "other" words, are predicted at zero. This program captures only the verb and "of"
part: about 4% of the variance on eval. A full per-word table gets roughly 10%, and most of the
rest is diffuse context that this short program does not capture.

Main program: look at the current word, and at the word before it in the same document.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

ACTIVITY_VERBS = frozenset(
    """read reading reads live lived lives living eat eating eats ate eaten drink drinking
    drinks drank drunk buy buying buys bought sell selling sells sold own owns owned owning
    wear wearing wears wore worn play playing plays played learn learning learns learned
    teach teaching teaches taught write writing writes wrote written publish publishing
    publishes published speak speaking speaks spoke spoken watch watching watches watched
    marry married cook cooking cooks cooked sing singing sings sang dance dancing drive
    driving drives drove purchase purchased purchasing install installed installing run
    running runs ran""".split()
)
CHINESE_ACTIVITY_VERBS = frozenset("穿 喝 吃 买 购买 饮 读 卖 住".split())
DETERMINERS = frozenset("the a an his her its their my your our this that these those".split())
PERSON_OR_MODAL = frozenset(
    "i you we he she they who people to can will would could should must may might also not".split()
)
OWNER_NOUNS = frozenset(
    "owner author copy copies sale sales proof execution release production delivery".split()
)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    if word in ACTIVITY_VERBS:
        if before in DETERMINERS:
            return carry, 0.5
        if before in PERSON_OR_MODAL:
            return carry, 6.0
        return carry, 2.5
    if word in CHINESE_ACTIVITY_VERBS:
        return carry, 4.0
    if word == "of":
        return carry, 3.0 if before in OWNER_NOUNS else 0.5
    return carry, 0.0

"""Negative activation on mathematical symbols, in math prose.

Layer 15's MLP down-projection component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1417
writes a negative value into the residual stream when the text is at a symbol that
stands for a quantity: a single Latin letter used as a variable (x, n, A, q), or the
token that opens a LaTeX math span ($, $$, \\(, ${).

It is strongest when the letter is introduced or named right after a word such as
"each x", "any n", "Let x", "where x", "the function f", "possible x", "integer n",
"matrix A". There it goes to about -2. A letter elsewhere goes to about -0.2, a
math opener to about -0.9. Everything else (words, digits, punctuation, code) is 0.

Caveat: the variance this captures is small (about 2% on eval). The component's
activation is mostly diffuse noise on ordinary tokens, which no simple rule here predicts.
"""

READS = ()

# Words after which a single letter is being introduced or named as a quantity.
MATH_INTRO = {
    "Let", "let", "where", "Where", "each", "any", "all", "possible", "function",
    "integer", "number", "matrix", "maximum", "minimum", "minimal", "length",
    "value", "vector", "point", "points", "equation", "compute", "set", "Since",
    "since", "find", "denote", "term", "sum", "size", "radius", "factor",
    "position", "variables", "$", "$$", "\\(", "${",
}

# LaTeX tokens that open a math span.
MATH_OPENERS = {" $", " $$", " \\(", " ${", " $\\", " $("}


def is_letter(s):
    """A single Latin letter, with an optional leading space."""
    s = s.strip()
    return len(s) == 1 and s.isascii() and s.isalpha()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if same_doc else ""
    if is_letter(cur):
        return carry, (-2.0 if prev in MATH_INTRO else -0.2)
    if cur in MATH_OPENERS:
        return carry, -0.9
    return carry, 0.0

"""p-82af68dd@100000 / layers.15.mlp.down_proj : 1418

A neuron-like component that fires on the period (".") that ends an abbreviation,
most strongly inside citations and references: journal, court and patent
abbreviations ("Chem.", "Tex. App.", "U.S. Pat.", "Vol.", "Fig.", "Cir.") and the
initials in author names ("J.", "S."). Sentence-ending periods after ordinary words,
and periods after digits, stay near zero. Most other tokens are predicted at zero.

The program reads only the word just before the period (in the same document) and
returns a value by its kind; it has no other state.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Abbreviations that mostly appear in bibliographic, legal and patent citations.
CITATION_ABBREVIATIONS = set(
    """Pat Vet App Art Vol Fig FIG Eq St Cir Ct Cal Tex Ann Rep Ed No Nos Sec Mag
    Soc Chem Phys Hist Bull Arch Zeitschr Rev Trans Proc Nat Gen Biol Med Sci J
    Acad Jahrb Abh Ber Bd Eng Lancet Anz Mitt Dist Supp Ser Pl Dr Mr Mrs""".split()
)


def abbreviation_kind(word):
    """0 citation abbreviation, 1 single capital (an initial), 2 other capitalised
    abbreviation, 3 short lowercase abbreviation, 4 anything else."""
    w = word.strip()
    if w in CITATION_ABBREVIATIONS:
        return 0
    if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z]", w):
        return 1
    if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z][A-Za-z]{0,3}", w) or re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z]{2,4}", w):
        return 2
    if re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]{1,4}", w):
        return 3
    return 4


# Mean activation after a period, by kind of word before it (fit on sampled training text).
VALUE = {0: 3.6, 1: 2.0, 2: 1.9, 3: 0.7, 4: 0.2}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if not token.startswith("."):
        return carry, 0.0
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and (
        prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    )
    word = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    return carry, VALUE[abbreviation_kind(word)]

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1419 (this component is that unit, scaled by ~1.07).

What it does, in plain terms: inside source code it swings. It goes clearly negative on
the whitespace and line-break tokens of code (the indentation that starts a line, and the
newline that ends a statement such as ');' or '()'), and mildly positive on tokens that
close a call mid-expression ('()', ').', ')'). In prose it stays near zero.

This program predicts those group means, using a code-density test on the document so far:
a document counts as code once more than 3% of its tokens contain code punctuation
({ } ; ( ) =). It explains only a little of the variance; the large swings are rare and
depend on context that a few token rules cannot see.
"""

import re

CODE_PUNCT = re.compile(r"[{};()=]")
CALL_CLOSE = (")", ").", "()", "().", ");", "();")
CODE_SHARE = 0.03
NEWLINE_OR_INDENT = -0.15
CALL_CLOSER = 0.08

READS = ()


def _is_indent_or_newline(token):
    return "\n" in token or (token.strip(" \t") == "" and token != "")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (tokens_so_far, code_tokens_so_far, document_id) for the current document
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[2] != doc:
        seen, code = 0, 0
    else:
        seen, code = carry[0], carry[1]
    in_code = seen > 0 and code / seen > CODE_SHARE
    seen += 1
    code += 1 if CODE_PUNCT.search(token) else 0
    value = 0.0
    if in_code:
        if _is_indent_or_newline(token):
            value = NEWLINE_OR_INDENT
        elif token in CALL_CLOSE:
            value = CALL_CLOSER
    return (seen, code, doc), float(value)

"""Predict the component's typical activation, with no real structure behind it.

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1420 is nearly inert: its causal
importance is essentially zero on every token, and switching it off changes the model's
next-token predictions by almost nothing. Its activation is a diffuse, noisy value
(mean about 0.064, std about 0.38). No token identity, token class (digit, punctuation,
space, letter) or position predicts it: a per-token lookup does not generalise to
held-out text, and position buckets explain under 0.1% of the variance.

So the program predicts the average value, 0.064, everywhere, except at the first token
of each document, where the activation is about 0.
"""

READS = ()

TYPICAL = 0.064


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids
    first = len(doc) == 1 or doc[-1] != doc[-2]
    return None, 0.0 if first else TYPICAL

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1421: a weak, token-class and document-start tilt.

The activation is a small signed value (std 0.34) with no strong driver. Token identity
alone explains about 2% of its variance on held-out text, and nothing simple we tried
explains much more: the program here explains well under 1%. It predicts two small
effects measured on training text:

- Token class: newlines and digits slightly positive, ordinary words slightly positive,
  punctuation slightly negative.
- Position in the document: the first few tokens of a document are pulled down, most
  sharply at positions 2 to 5, and the effect fades by about 20 tokens in.

Most of the variance is left unexplained.
"""

READS = ()

# mean activation per token class, measured on 4096 training rows
CLASS_MEAN = {
    "newline": 0.055,
    "digits": 0.039,
    "cjk": 0.035,
    "word": 0.024,
    "space": 0.003,
    "punct": -0.018,
    "partial": -0.012,
}

# offset from the class mean by position within the document (0 is its first token)
POSITION_OFFSET = [(0, 2, -0.015), (2, 6, -0.10), (6, 20, -0.06), (20, 100, -0.008)]


def token_class(text):
    if "�" in text:  # a fragment of a multi-byte character
        return "partial"
    if text.strip() == "":
        return "newline" if "\n" in text else "space"
    if text.strip().isdigit():
        return "digits"
    if any("一" <= ch <= "鿿" for ch in text):
        return "cjk"
    if any(ch.isalnum() for ch in text):
        return "word"
    return "punct"


def position_offset(n):
    for lo, hi, offset in POSITION_OFFSET:
        if lo <= n < hi:
            return offset
    return 0.007 if n >= 100 else 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (tokens so far in this document, document label of the last token)
    count, doc = carry if carry is not None else (0, None)
    label = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if label != doc:
        count = 0  # a new document starts here
    value = CLASS_MEAN[token_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])] + position_offset(count)
    return (count + 1, label), value

What it does: its activation is a dense, roughly symmetric signal (std about 0.3, largest about 2)

"""

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1424 (the down_proj component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1424).

What it does, in plain terms: the unit is mostly quiet, but it goes negative at clause
boundaries (commas, periods, semicolons) inside a sentence that hedges or qualifies, such
as "I'm not sure, ...", "Although its origins are ...", "... depends on the exact ...".
Those are the places where the next words are likely to be a contrast or a caveat
("but", "however", "depends on"). Its output pushes the next-token distribution toward
"but"/"however" when it is negative.

This program is the simple rule for that: it keeps one flag per sentence, set when a
hedge or contrast word has appeared since the last sentence end. At a clause boundary it
predicts a small negative value, and a larger negative one when the flag is set. Every
other token is predicted as 0. Document starts reset the flag.

Limits, measured on eval: this explains very little of the unit's variance (about 1%,
Pearson r about 0.1). Most of its variance sits in ordinary words and in contexts a
word list does not capture, so a lookup over words does not do much better.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that hedge, qualify or set up a contrast.
HEDGE_WORDS = frozenset(
    "although though however but while whilst whereas yet depends depending depend "
    "vary varies varied different differ unclear unknown unsure sure definite exact "
    "difficult limited may might possibly perhaps not".split()
)

# Predicted value at each clause boundary: commas and periods a little, semicolons more.
CLAUSE_END = {",": -0.1, ".": -0.1, ";": -0.35}

# Extra negative value at a clause boundary when the sentence so far has hedged.
HEDGED_EXTRA = -0.5


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]

BODY_AFTER_BRACE = -2.0
BODY_AFTER_COLON = -1.0
CODE_SCALE = 3.0  # the scale is CODE_SCALE times the share of code-like recent tokens


def _is_indent(tok):
    return tok != "" and tok.strip() == "" and "\n" not in tok


def _code_like(tok):
    return _is_indent(tok) or any(c in tok for c in "{};()[]<>=")


def _fresh():
    return {"line": "", "line_start": True, "in_header": False, "header_strength": 0.0,
            "opener": None, "header": 0.0, "recent": []}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    new_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    st = _fresh() if carry is None or new_doc else carry
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = tok.strip()
    closes = "{" in tok or tok.rstrip().endswith(":") or ";" in tok

    recent = (st["recent"] + [_code_like(tok)])[-RECENT:]
    scale = CODE_SCALE * sum(recent) / len(recent)

    if st["in_header"]:  # inside a keyword header, before its body opens
        value = -st["header_strength"] if closes else SIG_INNER
    elif st["line_start"] and word in HEADER_STRENGTH:  # the keyword that opens a header
        value = SIG_START
    elif _is_indent(tok) and st["line"] == "" and st["opener"]:  # first indent of a body
        value = {"header": BODY_AFTER_HEADER, "brace": BODY_AFTER_BRACE,
                 "colon": BODY_AFTER_COLON}[st["opener"]]
    elif closes and st["header"] > 0:  # a brace or colon right after a header line
        value = -st["header"]
    else:
        value = 0.0

    # update the state with this token
    if st["in_header"]:
        if closes:
            st["in_header"] = False
    elif st["line_start"] and word in HEADER_STRENGTH:
        st["in_header"] = True
        st["header_strength"] = HEADER_STRENGTH[word]
    if "\n" in tok:  # a line ended: remember how it ended and whether it was a header
        full = st["line"] + tok.split("\n")[0]
        if full.strip():
            end = full.rstrip()[-1:]
            strength = max([HEADER_STRENGTH.get(w, 0.0) for w in full.split()] + [0.0])
            st["opener"] = "header" if strength >= 3 and end in "{:" else (
                "brace" if end == "{" else ("colon" if end == ":" else None))
            st["header"] = strength if end in "{:" else 0.0
        st["line"] = tok.split("\n")[-1]
        st["line_start"] = True
    else:
        st["line"] += tok
        if word:
            st["line_start"] = False
    st["recent"] = recent
    return st, float(value * scale)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1455: a diffuse, token-independent offset.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of layers.15.mlp.down_proj. Its activation is
(hidden . V[:, 1455]) * ||U[:, 1455]||. Most of V's weight sits on MLP hidden unit 1455
(about 41% of its squared norm), with smaller weights on a few hundred other units, so the
activation is roughly a readout of that one hidden unit of layer 15's MLP.

What it responds to: nothing readable. Across 16k training rows (about 8M tokens) the
activation is roughly symmetric around a small positive mean (0.045), with std 0.33 and
no clear token, position, or previous-token pattern. Knowing the current token explains
about 1% of its variance, the previous token nothing, and position almost nothing. Its
causal importance is essentially zero everywhere, and switching it off barely changes the
model's next-token predictions.

So the program predicts the component's mean activation at every position. This is the
best constant in variance-explained terms and keeps the average output shift minimal. It
explains none of the variance; the simple concept-based alternatives we tried explain at
most about 1%.
"""

READS = ()

# The component's mean activation over training positions.
MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.045


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Return the constant mean activation at this position (no state is carried)."""
    return None, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1457, a weak, mostly context-driven readout.

What it is: the component's activation is (MLP hidden vector . V_c) * ||U_c||. Its V_c is
almost entirely the MLP hidden unit 1457 of layer 15 (about 0.6 of its 0.86 norm), so the
activation tracks that one hidden unit. That unit is strongly context-dependent: it is
large and positive on Chinese words that continue a clause, and large and negative on
English and other-language coordinating conjunctions ("and", "or", "but", "und", "и", ...)
in some contexts, not all.

What this program does: a lexical approximation. It looks only at the newest token and
predicts the average sign of the activation for two word classes:
  - Chinese coordinating words (并, 和, 而, 后, ...): a small positive value.
  - Coordinating conjunctions in English and other languages (and, or, but, und, и, ...),
    and the Chinese enumeration comma 、: a small negative value.
Every other token predicts 0.

Honest limit: this explains almost none of the variance (about 0.1% on training rows). Token
identity alone explains about 1%, and no combination of word classes, scripts, positions or
document-level features tested explains much more. The activation depends on the surrounding
context in a way a short rule cannot capture, so this is a readable sketch of the direction
of the effect, not a faithful model of it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Chinese words that join clauses or phrases (并 "and also", 和 "and", 而 "and yet", 后 "after").
ZH_COORDINATORS = {"并", "和", "而", "后", "与", "及", "且", "或", "以及", "然后", "但是", "因此", "所以"}

# Coordinating conjunctions in English and other languages, plus the Chinese enumeration comma.
CONJUNCTIONS = {"and", "or", "but", "nor", "yet", "und", "и", "و", "а", "、", "&"}

ZH_VALUE = 0.25
CONJ_VALUE = -0.05


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Predict the component's activation at the newest token from that token alone."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in ZH_COORDINATORS:
        return carry, ZH_VALUE
    if word in CONJUNCTIONS:
        return carry, CONJ_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Statistical p-value numbers (layer 15, MLP hidden unit 1458, read through down_proj).

What it does: this component fires on the number inside a reported p-value, such as the
"047" of "P = 0.047" or the ".012" of "p = .012". Its biggest responses are on the first
decimal digit after "0." (and on the "." after a bare "0" in "P = 0."); later decimal
digits fire less. The "P" or "p" itself, and the "=" or "<" right after it, fire a little.

It responds only when the text is a statistics report: words such as "groups", "patients",
"significant" and "difference" nearby. In maths ("p = 0." or a citation "p. 53") it stays
near zero. Everywhere else it is near zero, a small diffuse background this program does not
model.

How it works: for each token it reads the last few tokens. If they form a standalone "P" or
"p", optionally "value", an optional comparison sign and the start of a decimal number, it
predicts the activation for the token just read from a table of values by digit position.
That value is scaled by how many statistics-report words appear in the previous 60 tokens
(a full scale from three such words).
"""

import re

READS = ()

# A standalone p or P, optional "value", then the number typed so far (ending at this token).
P_NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z])[pP]\s*(?:value\s*)?[=<>≤≥¼]?\s*(\d*\.?\d*)$")
# A standalone p or P, optional "value", ending right before the current token.
P_BEFORE = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z])[pP]\s*(?:value\s*)?$")

# Vocabulary of statistical reporting.
STATS_WORDS = {
    "p", "significant", "significantly", "significance", "statistically", "difference",
    "differences", "group", "groups", "patients", "control", "trial", "study", "cohort",
    "participants", "effect", "treatment", "compared", "versus", "mean", "ci", "sd",
    "correlation", "odds", "ratio", "analysis", "between", "respectively",
}

SIGNS = {"=", "<", ">", "≤", "≥", "¼"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    recent = [
        s for s, d in zip(prefix.token_strings[-12:], prefix.document_ids[-12:]) if d == doc
    ]
    token = recent[-1].strip()
    before = "".join(recent[:-1])

    # How much statistical-report vocabulary is nearby, scaled from 0 to 1.
    context = [
        s.strip().lower()
        for s, d in zip(prefix.token_strings[-60:], prefix.document_ids[-60:])
        if d == doc
    ]
    ramp = min(sum(1 for w in context if w in STATS_WORDS), 3) / 3

    if token in ("P", "p"):
        return carry, 1.0 * ramp  # the p itself
    if token in SIGNS and P_BEFORE.search(before):
        return carry, 5.0 * ramp  # the sign straight after p

    m = P_NUMBER.search("".join(recent))
    if not m:
        return carry, 0.0
    number = m.group(1)  # the number typed so far, including this token
    if number in ("0.", "."):
        base = 9.0  # the point after a bare 0 in "P = 0."
    elif re.fullmatch(r"0\.\d", number):
        base = 20.0  # the first decimal digit of "P = 0.x"
    elif re.fullmatch(r"\.\d", number):
        base = 17.0  # the first decimal digit of "P = .x"
    elif re.fullmatch(r"0?\.\d{2,}", number):
        base = 6.0  # later decimal digits
    else:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, base * ramp

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1459, read through one down_proj component.

Nearly all of this component's activation is the MLP hidden unit 1459 of layer 15 (its
direction in the MLP's hidden space is 0.68 on that unit, and small everywhere else), scaled
by about 1.09. Its size is diffuse: it has std 0.35 at every position, and the token
identity, the previous token, the next token, and position in the document each explain
almost none of it (under 3% together, even with a large lookup table).

What the largest values look like, in the sample we measured:
  * negative: prepositions and clause-linking words that take an object or a time/place
    ("on", "upon", "into", "through", "during", "when", "then", "as", "about"), e.g.
    "the first vertex (a, 0) is [on] the axis", "is [given] the right to".
  * positive: comparison words ("than" after "rather", "higher", "faster", "different";
    "compared [to]", "versus", "another", "others", "from"), e.g. "compared [to] the
    standard", "larger [than] the other".

This program predicts those two word classes with their average activation and 0 elsewhere.
It explains very little of the variance (well under 1%); the bulk of the activation is not
captured by any word-level rule we found.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Comparison and contrast words: their average activation is slightly positive.
COMPARISON = {" than", " versus", " vs", " unlike", " another", " others", " other", " rather", " from", " against", " to"}
COMPARISON_VALUE = 0.02

# Locative, temporal and clause-linking prepositions: their average activation is negative.
LOCATIVE = {" on", " upon", " into", " through", " during", " when", " then", " about", " as", " at", " over", " after"}
LOCATIVE_VALUE = -0.09


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = prefix.token_strings[prefix.position]
    if word in COMPARISON:
        return carry, COMPARISON_VALUE
    if word in LOCATIVE:
        return carry, LOCATIVE_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1460: a weak, mostly unexplained tendency.

The component's activation is (MLP hidden vector x its direction V) times ||U||. Almost all of
its variance is context-dependent and diffuse: no token, previous token, next token, position
or document-level feature predicts it well (held-out R^2 of the best token-level tables is about
0.02; of the readable rules below, about 0.002). Its main single input is MLP hidden unit 1460,
but that unit has no clean concept either.

What this program does: it predicts the three consistent token-class averages that were
measured on training text:
  - chat-template and tool markers (<|im_start|>, <think>, </think>, <tool_call>, ...): about -0.19
  - the negation words "no" and "not": about +0.06
  - the digits 0-9: about -0.03
and 0 for every other token. It is a readable summary of the small tendencies, not a model of
the component's variance.
"""

READS = ()

CHAT_MARKERS = {
    "<|im_start|>", "<|im_end|>", "<think>", "</think>",
    "<tool_call>", "</tool_call>", "<tool_response>", "</tool_response>",
}
NEGATION_WORDS = {"no", "not", " no", " not", " No", " Not"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token in CHAT_MARKERS:
        return carry, -0.19
    if token in NEGATION_WORDS:
        return carry, 0.06
    if token in DIGITS:
        return carry, -0.03
    return carry, 0.0

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1461 (a dense, context-driven direction).

What it does: this rank-one piece reads the MLP hidden state of layer 15 along one fixed
direction and writes it back into the residual stream. Its activation is dense, not sparse:
std about 0.68 over all tokens, and it is almost never important to the model's output
(its causal importance passes 0.1 on about 0.007% of tokens).

What this program captures: almost nothing, honestly. Token identity, token class (digits,
newlines, CJK, punctuation), the previous tokens, repetition within a document, and the
document or row as a whole explain well under 1% of its variance. The one real effect found
is position within a document: the first token of each document sits near 0, the second
token is strongly negative (about -0.5), and the next few are progressively less negative
until the activation settles near its overall mean (about +0.05) from roughly the 5th token on.

So the program predicts that position profile and a constant mean otherwise. It needs one
piece of state, the current document's id and the position counted within it.
"""

READS = ()

# Mean activation at each position within a document (0 = its first token), measured on
# training rows. Positions from 5 onward sit near the overall mean, so they share one value.
EARLY = {0: 0.0, 1: -0.53, 2: -0.28, 3: -0.14, 4: -0.07}
LATER = 0.05


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the activation at the newest token from its position in its document."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        k = 0  # first token of a new document (or of the row)
    else:
        k = carry[1] + 1
    return (doc, k), EARLY.get(k, LATER)

"""Assignment operators in code.

The component is nearly silent on most tokens, but it goes negative on the " =" (and " +=")
that assigns to a variable. The more code-like the last 100 tokens are, the more negative
it is, and it is more negative still after "]" (an indexed assignment such as a[i] = x).
Everything else predicts 0. This captures only a small part of the variance: its largest
negative values are rare and depend on finer context (e.g. a variable reassigned from itself)."""
from collections import deque

READS = ()

WINDOW = 100
CODE_MARKS = set(";{}[]()<>")
ASSIGN_OPS = {" =", " +="}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if carry is None or new_doc:
        carry = deque(maxlen=WINDOW)
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if not new_doc else ""
    value = 0.0
    if tok in ASSIGN_OPS:
        density = sum(carry) / max(len(carry), 1)
        value = -0.3 - 8.0 * density
        if prev == "]":
            value -= 2.5
    carry.append(1 if any(c in CODE_MARKS for c in tok) else 0)
    return carry, value

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):

"""Layer 15 MLP neuron 1467 (component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1467).

Rough description: the component is essentially MLP hidden unit 1467 of layer 15
(its read vector is ~0.65 on that unit). Its activation is a weak, diffuse signal:
it tends to dip negative on mathematical notation (variables, brackets, operators,
LaTeX) when that notation is dense, and is near zero in ordinary prose.

This program predicts a small negative value on math-looking tokens that sit in a
math-dense stretch of text (at least 40% of the last 16 tokens are math-looking),
and 0 elsewhere. It is a crude description: it explains almost none of the variance.
"""
import re
from collections import deque

READS = ()

MATH_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z]|\d+|[\\^_{}()\[\]=+\-*/<>|]+|\\[A-Za-z]+|sin|cos|tan|log|ln|exp")
WINDOW = 16
DENSE = 0.4
SCALE = -0.02


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        flags = deque(maxlen=WINDOW)
    else:
        flags = carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    is_math = bool(MATH_TOKEN.fullmatch(token))
    flags.append(is_math)
    density = sum(flags) / len(flags)
    value = SCALE if is_math and density >= DENSE else 0.0
    return (doc, flags), value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1468 (its down_proj component), read as a word-level feature.

The component is a rank-one piece that reads almost only MLP hidden unit 1468 of layer 15.
Its activation is mostly small and context-dependent, with a typical value slightly below
zero (about -0.03). What it does respond to, on word level:

- Negative, the strong side: words about a person's own identity and self. Examples:
  personal, individual, identity, privacy, profile, portrait, biography, birthday, photo,
  avatar, name, account, user / username, person, and reflexive pronouns (himself, herself,
  yourself, myself). Strongest on "personal", "portrait", "avatar" and "profile" (-1 to -3).
- Positive, the weaker side: words about age and stage of life. Examples: young, younger,
  elderly, aged, former, retired, oldest, youth, prison (about +0.3 to +1).
- Everything else sits near a small baseline, and the first token of each document is 0.

This program reads only the current token, so it is causal and stateless. It predicts a
fixed value per word class, the baseline elsewhere, and 0 at each document's first token.
It explains only a small share of the variance: most of the activation is a diffuse,
context-dependent spread that no word list captures.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Stems matched inside the lower-cased token, with "_" removed (so "_user" and "User" match).
SELF_STEMS = (
    "user", "profile", "personal", "person", "avatar", "identity", "privacy",
    "individual", "portrait", "biograph", "photo", "birthday", "email", "name", "account",
    "himself", "herself", "yourself", "myself", "ourselves", "themselves",
)
AGE_STEMS = ("young", "elder", "former", "retire", "aged", "oldest", "prison", "youth")

BASELINE = -0.025  # the activation's mean on ordinary tokens
SELF_VALUE = -0.55  # mean activation on self/identity words is about -0.5 to -1.6
AGE_VALUE = 0.33  # mean activation on age words is about +0.3 to +0.6


def _has(token: str, stems: tuple[str, ...]) -> bool:
    word = token.strip().lower().replace("_", "")
    return any(stem in word for stem in stems)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    if len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0  # a document's first token: the activation is about zero there
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if _has(token, SELF_STEMS):
        return carry, SELF_VALUE
    if _has(token, AGE_STEMS):
        return carry, AGE_VALUE
    return carry, BASELINE

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1469 (the component), as a short rule.

The unit goes strongly negative on a word that joins two parallel items: "X and Y",
"X or Y", and the same words in other languages (und, oder, и, et, 和, 或, &). The
size depends on the word just before the conjunction. After an adjective or verb
("simple and", "create or") it is most negative; after a plain noun less so; after a
comma or a closing bracket or quote it is close to zero. "or", "oder" and "und" are
about 1.4 times as strong as "and". Every other token is zero.

On held-out rows the rule explains about 7% of the unit's variance (Pearson r about
0.26). Most of its variation is a long tail of very negative values on conjunctions
that this rule cannot separate from ordinary ones, so the rule captures the typical
size, not the extremes.
"""

import wordnet

READS = ()

CONJUNCTIONS = {" and", " or", "/or", " und", " oder", " и", " et", " &", "和", "或"}
STRONG = {" or", " oder", " und", "/or"}
CLOSING = {",", ")", "]", "}", '"', "”", "'"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token not in CONJUNCTIONS or len(prefix.token_strings) < 2:
        return carry, 0.0
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip()
    if before in CLOSING:
        size = 0.2
    elif before.isascii() and before.isalpha():
        size = 0.9 if wordnet.parts_of_speech(before.lower()) == {"noun"} else 2.2
    else:
        size = 0.8
    if token in STRONG:
        size *= 1.4
    return carry, -size

"""Negation neuron: MLP hidden unit 1470 of layer 15, read as a rule about negated phrases.

The component is one rank-one piece of layers.15.mlp.down_proj. Its read direction is
dominated by that hidden unit (weight 0.84 of norm 1.08), so its activation is about
0.9 times the unit's value silu(gate) * up. Measured: correlation 0.70 overall, 0.99 on
the large values.
What the data shows:
- The negation words ("not", "no", "never", "cannot", "nor", "neither", "none", "without",
  "non", "n't", "nothing") and the exclusive words "only", "instead", "else" are negative
  on average, about -0.3 to -0.4.
- Words that sit 2 to 6 tokens after a negation word, in the same document, are a little
  positive on average.
- Large values (|activation| above 2) sit inside negated phrases ("not directly",
  "cannot ... on our own"), and need the gate open. Their sign follows the up projection,
  which no word list captures: about three in four are positive, but the sign varies
  from token to token. This program does not predict that sign.
- Most of the variance is a diffuse background of small values with no token pattern.
Everything else is predicted as 0. Measured on eval it explains about 0.2% of the
variance, so it is a weak description of this component.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

NEGATORS = frozenset(
    {"not", "no", "never", "cannot", "nor", "neither", "none", "without", "non", "n't", "nothing"}
)
EXCLUSIVES = frozenset({"only", "instead", "else"})
SCOPE = 6  # how many tokens after a negation word still count as inside its phrase
FIRST, EXCLUSIVE_VALUE, NEGATED_VALUE, NEGATOR_VALUE = 2, -0.35, 0.1, -0.3


def word(text: str) -> str:
    """A token's text, lower-cased, with the curly apostrophe made straight."""
    return text.strip().lower().replace("’", "'")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    doc = prefix.document_ids[t]
    here = word(prefix.token_strings[t])
    if here in NEGATORS:
        return carry, NEGATOR_VALUE
    if here in EXCLUSIVES:
        return carry, EXCLUSIVE_VALUE
    # Look back over the tokens of this document for a negation word a few tokens earlier.
    for j in range(t - FIRST, max(-1, t - SCOPE - 1), -1):
        if prefix.document_ids[j] != doc:
            break
        if word(prefix.token_strings[j]) in NEGATORS:
            return carry, NEGATED_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 1471 (the down_proj component 1471), predicted from word classes.

The unit is near zero on most tokens and dips negative on some of them. Averaged
by kind of token, it is most negative on chat-template and markup tokens
(<|im_start|>, <|endoftext|>, <tool_call>), then on non-Latin-script text, on
clause-joining words (and, but, that, if, because), on punctuation and line
breaks. It is slightly positive on English articles and auxiliary verbs (a, the,
are, was, can). This program gives each class one fixed value and gives 0 at the
first token of every document, where the unit is always quiet.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

CONJUNCTIONS = set(
    "and or but if that which because so as when while although than whether "
    "since until unless such how".split()
)
ARTICLES = {"a", "an", "the", "this", "these", "those"}
AUXILIARIES = set(
    "is are was were be been being am can could will would should may might "
    "must do does did has have had".split()
)
PRONOUNS = set(
    "i you he she it we they me him her us them my your his its our their "
    "who whom whose what".split()
)

# Mean activation per class, from about 8 million training tokens.
MEAN = {
    "special": -0.32,
    "nonlatin": -0.14,
    "conj": -0.11,
    "ws": -0.11,
    "other": -0.11,
    "digit": -0.08,
    "word": -0.07,
    "punct": -0.09,
    "pron": -0.05,
    "article": 0.01,
    "aux": 0.02,
}


def word_class(token):
    """The class of one token, from its text alone."""
    s = token.strip().lower()
    if s.startswith("<|") or regex.fullmatch(r"</?[a-z_]+>", s):
        return "special"
    if regex.search(r"[\p{Han}\p{Arabic}\p{Cyrillic}\p{Hiragana}\p{Katakana}\p{Hangul}]|，|、", token):
        return "nonlatin"
    if not s:
        return "ws"
    if s.isdigit():
        return "digit"
    if s in CONJUNCTIONS:
        return "conj"
    if s in ARTICLES:
        return "article"
    if s in AUXILIARIES:
        return "aux"
    if s in PRONOUNS:
        return "pron"
    if not any(ch.isalnum() for ch in s):
        return "punct"
    if s.isalpha():
        return "word"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """carry: the document id of the previous token (None at a row's start)."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is not None and carry != doc:
        return doc, 0.0  # a new document starts here: the unit is quiet
    return doc, MEAN[word_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])]
